lesson.title: The X-Intercept: Where a Line Touches Ground Level
lesson.summary: The x-intercept is the point where a line's graph crosses the horizontal axis, found algebraically by setting y equal to zero and solving for x.
lesson.body:
Every point sitting on the horizontal axis shares one feature in common: a y-coordinate of zero. This was established back when quadrants and the origin were first introduced, since points with y = 0 are exactly the ones that fail to be above or below the axis at all, sitting right along it instead. The x-intercept of a line is the specific point where that line's graph crosses the horizontal axis, so by definition, it is the one point on the line where y = 0. A line can have at most one x-intercept, unless the line is horizontal itself, in which case it either overlaps the axis entirely or never touches it.

Because the y-coordinate is already known to be zero at this crossing point, finding the x-intercept algebraically is just a matter of substitution. Take the equation of the line, replace y with 0, and solve the resulting equation for x. Whatever value of x makes that equation true is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept, and the full point is written as (x, 0), with the y-coordinate always fixed at zero by definition. This substitution step is the same idea used whenever a function is evaluated at a specific input, except here the known quantity is the output instead of the input, so the equation has to be solved rather than simply computed.

Here is a worked example using the line from the previous chapter, y = 3x - 2. To find where this line crosses the horizontal axis, set y equal to 0: 0 = 3x - 2. Add 2 to both sides: 2 = 3x. Divide both sides by 3: x = 2/3. So the x-intercept is the point (2/3, 0). To check this answer, substitute x = 2/3 back into the original equation and confirm that y really does come out to 0: y = 3(2/3) - 2 = 2 - 2 = 0. The check confirms the x-intercept was found correctly, and the algebra holds together cleanly at every step.

Notice that this point, (2/3, 0), should lie on the same straight line already graphed using the points (0, -2), (1, 1), (2, 4), and (3, 7) from the previous chapter. Since 2/3 falls between 0 and 1, the x-intercept should land on the line somewhere between the points for x = 0 and x = 1, which matches the fact that the line crosses from a negative y-value at x = 0 to a positive y-value at x = 1, passing through zero somewhere in that stretch, exactly as expected for a continuously rising straight line.

X-intercepts are especially useful landmarks because they are quick to locate on a graph just by looking for where the line physically touches the horizontal axis, and quick to calculate algebraically by setting y to 0. In applied problems, an x-intercept often marks a meaningful boundary, such as the moment a quantity that was decreasing finally reaches zero, for example when a tank of water measured over time finally empties out completely. Together with the y-intercept, covered next, these two crossing points give a fast, reliable way to sketch or verify the graph of almost any line.
